title: Binary Search Tree
html:
A binary search tree keeps its keys ordered: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller, everything in its right subtree is larger. That one invariant is what every problem here exploits — the inorder traversal is sorted, every search is a single root-to-leaf walk, and a count stored in each node turns order statistics into O(h) queries.

Binary Search Tree (BST) — a binary tree in which, for every node, all keys in the left subtree are < the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are > it. The rule applies to whole subtrees, not just to the two children — this is the detail most wrong solutions miss.

What the problems rely on

The reader already knows search, insert and delete. The advanced problems are built from four consequences of the BST invariant:

Inorder is sorted

Left, node, right visits keys in ascending order. Anything you can do on a sorted array (two pointers, previous-element checks, kth element) you can do on a BST without materialising the array.

One path answers a query

Search, floor, ceiling, predecessor and successor each follow a single root-to-leaf path: O(h) time, where h is the height.

Ancestors bound a node

A node must lie strictly inside the range (lower, upper) set by all of its ancestors — not only by its parent.

Nodes can carry extra data

Storing the size of the left subtree (an augmented BST) makes “kth smallest” and “rank of x” O(h) queries.

OperationTimeNote
search / insert / deleteO(h)h = O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed
floor / ceiling / successorO(h)one path down, remember the best candidate
kth smallest (plain)O(h + k)inorder traversal stopped after k nodes
kth smallest (augmented)O(h)each node stores the size of its left subtree
check if a tree is a BSTO(n)range method or inorder-previous method
inorder traversalO(n)stack holds at most h nodes
Key point

The library ordered containers — C++ std::set / std::map, Java TreeSet / TreeMap — are self-balancing BSTs (red-black trees), so h = O(log n) is guaranteed. Python and JavaScript ship no ordered set; you either write a small BST, keep a sorted list with bisect (O(n) inserts) or use a third-party package.

Floor and ceiling of a key

Example

Input: tree A, x = 11
Output: floor 10, ceiling 12
Input: tree A, x = 23
Output: floor 22, ceiling -1 (none)
Input: tree A, x = 3
Output: floor -1 (none), ceiling 4

Idea

Walk down from the root. For the floor (largest key <= x): when the current key is too big go left; when it is <= x it is a candidate — record it and go right to look for a closer one. The ceiling is the mirror image. The answer is the last candidate recorded on the path — no backtracking, no recursion.

Time O(h)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Returning as soon as you see a key <= x gives a valid floor but not the greatest one — floor(11) would stop at 8 instead of continuing right to 10. Always keep walking and overwrite the candidate.

Ceiling on the left side of every element

Example

Input: arr = [2, 8, 30, 15, 25, 12]
Output: -1 -1 -1 30 30 15
Input: arr = [30, 20, 10]
Output: -1 30 20

For every arr[i], print the smallest element among arr[0..i-1] that is >= arr[i], or -1 if there is none. The first element never has one.

The obvious solution rescans the prefix for each element:

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Idea

Keep the elements seen so far in an ordered set (a self-balancing BST). The ceiling of arr[i] is then one O(log n) query — lower_bound in C++, TreeSet.ceiling in Java — and inserting arr[i] afterwards is another. Python uses bisect on a sorted list (the query is O(log n), the insert O(n) but with a very small constant); JavaScript reuses the hand-written BST from the previous section.

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)
Key point

Query before insert: if you insert arr[i] first, its own ceiling is itself and every answer becomes arr[i]. The same pattern (ordered set of the prefix + one query per element) solves floor on the left, ceiling on the right (scan from the end) and count of smaller elements to the left.

Kth smallest element

Example

Input: tree A, k = 3
Output: 10
Input: tree A, k = 7
Output: 22
Input: tree A, k = 8
Output: -1 (fewer than 8 nodes)

Idea

Inorder visits keys in ascending order, so the kth node visited is the kth smallest. Run an iterative inorder traversal with an explicit stack, count the nodes as they are popped, and stop as soon as the count reaches k — no need to finish the traversal.

Time O(h + k)Space O(h)
Pitfall

The original notes used a recursive traversal with a global counter and a return after printing — but the return only leaves the current frame, the parent frames continue into their right subtrees, and the counter is never reset for a second query. An explicit stack (or a counter object passed down and a boolean found flag) avoids both bugs.

When the tree is queried many times, or k is large, pay a little memory to make every query O(h): store in each node the number of nodes in its left subtree (lcount). Insert maintains it — every time the new key goes left, the node it passes gains one left descendant.

Time O(h)Space O(1)
Key point

The same lcount field answers rank(x) (how many keys are < x) in O(h), and n - k + 1 turns kth smallest into kth largest. If the tree also supports delete, every node on the deletion path whose left subtree shrank must have its lcount decremented — forgetting that silently corrupts later queries.

Check whether a binary tree is a BST

Example

Input: tree A
Output: Yes
Input: tree B
Output: No

The tempting solution compares each node with its two children only. It accepts tree B:

Avoid

8 < 20, 4 < 8 < 25, 20 < 22 — every local check passes, yet 25 is in the left subtree of 20. The BST rule constrains a node by all of its ancestors, not just its parent.

A correct but slow fix checks, for every node, the maximum of the whole left subtree and the minimum of the whole right subtree. Each node is scanned by each of its ancestors, which is O(n²) on a skewed tree:

Time O(n²) worst caseSpace O(h)
Idea

Range method. Pass down the open interval (lo, hi) that the ancestors allow. The root may be anything; going left tightens hi to the current key, going right tightens lo. Each node is visited once and checked against two numbers — O(n).

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Using INT_MIN / INT_MAX as the initial bounds with int keys rejects a tree that legitimately contains INT_MIN or INT_MAX (the check is strict). Use a wider type for the bounds (long long / long), ±Infinity in JavaScript, or None sentinels meaning unbounded.

Idea

Inorder-previous method. Inorder of a BST is strictly increasing. Traverse inorder and remember the previous key; the moment the current key is <= the previous one, the tree is not a BST. One pass, no bounds, and it stops at the first violation.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Key point

Both methods use a strict comparison, so a tree with duplicate keys is rejected. If your definition allows duplicates on one side (say left <= node), relax exactly that one bound — and say so in the interview before you code.

Fix a BST with two nodes swapped

Example

Input: tree above
Output: inorder before: 4 60 10 20 8 80 100, after: 4 8 10 20 60 80 100

Idea

The inorder sequence of a BST is sorted; swapping two keys creates one or two dips (a place where a key is smaller than its predecessor). With two dips, the swapped nodes are the larger element of the first dip and the smaller element of the second; with one dip (the two nodes are inorder-adjacent) they are the two elements of that dip. Record first at the first dip and overwrite second at every dip, then swap their keys.

1
Traverse inorder, remembering prev
At each node compare node.key with prev.key.
2
First dip (node.key < prev.key)
Set first = prev and second = node.
3
Second dip
Only second = node changes — first stays the larger element of the first dip.
4
Swap
Exchange first.key and second.key. The structure of the tree is untouched.
Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Setting second = prev at the second dip (instead of second = node) picks the wrong node. Trace the adjacent case too: in 8 / 20 22 (the root 20 swapped with its child 8) the inorder is 20 8 22 — a single dip, so first = 20, second = 8, and the single swap is correct. The original notes kept prev/first/second as globals, which breaks as soon as the function is called twice; the Fixer object above resets them per call.

Pair with a given sum in a BST

Example

Input: tree A, sum = 30
Output: Yes (8 + 22, or 10 + 20)
Input: tree A, sum = 29
Output: No

Idea

Method 1 — inorder + two pointers. Inorder gives the keys sorted. Then the classic sorted-array trick: a pointer at each end, move the left one right when the sum is too small and the right one left when it is too large. O(n) time, O(n) for the array.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Idea

Method 2 — hash set during the traversal. Visit the nodes (inorder here, but any order works) and keep the keys seen so far in a set. At each node ask whether target - key has already been seen; if not, add key. This is exactly the array “pair sum with hashing” solution, run on the tree in place. It reports a different (equally valid) pair than the two-pointer method — 10 + 20 is complete as soon as 20 is visited, before 22 is reached.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

Both methods are O(n) time and O(n) extra space. The O(h) space version runs the two-pointer idea directly on the tree: one stack performs a forward inorder (left-node-right) and a second stack a reverse inorder (right-node-left); advance whichever side the two-pointer rule says to move. It is the same algorithm with the sorted array replaced by two lazy iterators.

Pitfall

target - node.key in seen must be checked before seen.add(node.key); otherwise a node pairs with itself when target = 2 * key (sum 40 would report 20 + 20 on tree A).

Interview Q&A

Why is the inorder traversal of a BST sorted?

Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. By the BST invariant everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything in the right subtree is larger, and the same holds recursively inside each subtree — so the sequence produced is ascending. Reverse inorder (right, node, left) gives descending order.

How do you find the kth smallest in O(h) when the tree changes over time?

Augment every node with the size of its left subtree. Insert and delete update that count along the single path they touch (O(h)), and the query walks down comparing k with lcount + 1. The plain inorder method is O(h + k) per query and needs no extra field — fine for one-off queries, not for a stream of them.

Why does comparing a node with its children not prove a tree is a BST?

Because the invariant constrains a node by all its ancestors. In tree B above, 25 is a valid right child of 8 but it lives in the left subtree of 20, where every key must be below 20. Pass down the (lo, hi) range from the ancestors, or check that the inorder sequence strictly increases — both are O(n).

Two nodes of a BST were swapped. How many dips can the inorder sequence have, and which nodes do you swap back?

One or two. If the swapped nodes are adjacent in inorder there is one dip and its two elements are the culprits. Otherwise there are two dips: the larger element of the first dip and the smaller element of the second. Recording first = prev only at the first dip and second = node at every dip handles both cases with one pass.

What are std::set, TreeMap and heapq in terms of BSTs?

std::set/std::map and Java's TreeSet/TreeMap are red-black trees — self-balancing BSTs with O(log n) insert, delete, lower_bound/ceiling, floor and ordered iteration. heapq is not a BST: a heap only exposes its minimum, so it cannot answer floor/ceiling or kth queries. Python and JavaScript have no ordered-set container in the standard library.

How would you find the lowest common ancestor of two keys in a BST?

Walk down from the root: if both keys are smaller go left, if both are larger go right, otherwise the current node is the split point and therefore the LCA. O(h) time, no parent pointers and no recursion needed — a general binary tree needs an O(n) traversal instead.
